The phone call was made by Joel Manuel, with the BOE, to Respondent on March 17,
2023. During the phone call, Mr. Manuel introduced himself to Respondent, and Mr. Manuel and
Respondent discussed a rifle that was donated to Respondent and used for a campaign raffle.
According to the phone call, the rifle was made of damaged or blemished parts that were sold
through a website “from time to time.” The phone call did not specify any dates that particular
parts were purchased or a date that the rifle was donated. During the phone call, Mr. Manuel stated
that he would email a Subpoena Duces Tecum (SDT) to Respondent.
The BOE did not call Mr. Thibodeaux, Mr. Smith, Mr. Manuel, or Respondent to testify.
The BOE prepared an SDT, addressed to Respondent, requesting documents covering the
period of January 1, 2022, through January 31, 2023.14
No evidence was offered defining the aggregating period for Respondent’s 2022 candidacy
for Chief of Police, Town of Pearl River.
As of February 5, 2025, Respondent had not filed any campaign finance disclosure report
with the BOE in connection with his 2022 candidacy for Chief of Police, Town of Pearl River.15
CONCLUSIONS OF LAW
The BOE failed to prove by clear and convincing evidence that Respondent was required
to file either a 10-P or a 10-G campaign finance disclosure report in connection with his 2022
candidacy for Chief of Police, Town of Pearl River. Because the BOE failed to prove that
Respondent was required to file a 10-P and a 10-G campaign finance disclosure report, it is not
authorized to impose upon Respondent any additional civil penalty in accordance with La. R.S.
18:1505.4(A)(4)(a) and (b).16
14 BOE-10.
15 BOE-9.
16 La. R.S. 18:1505.4(A)(4)(a) and (b) of the CFDA provides that, if after conducting an adjudicatory hearing, the
EAB determines that a candidate knowingly failed to file the required 10-P report, or filed the 10-P report more than
5

In hearings under the CFDA before the EAB, the BOE must prove by clear and convincing
evidence that the candidate was required to and knowingly failed to timely file a required campaign
finance disclosure report.17 Failure to timely file any required report is a violation of the CFDA.18
The office of Chief of Police, Town of Pearl River, is an “any other” level public office.
Every candidate for an “any other” level public office (or the campaign treasurer) is required to
file with the BOE campaign finance disclosure reports of contributions and/or expenditures only
if he (a) has campaign expenditures in excess of $2,500, or (b) receives a campaign contribution
in excess of $200 in the aggregate during the aggregating period.19
Because the office of Chief of Police, Town of Pearl River is an “any other” level public
office, Respondent, in connection with his 2022 candidacy, was subject to the campaign finance
disclosure reporting requirement if he (a) spent more than $2,500 on his campaign or (b) received
a campaign contribution in excess of $200 in the aggregate during the aggregating period.
The BOE does not allege that Respondent made expenditures in excess of $2,500. The
BOE contends that Respondent triggered the 10-P and 10-G reporting requirements because he
received a campaign contribution in excess of $200, specifically, a rifle with an alleged value of
approximately $300. The BOE’s contention is not supported by the evidence.
The BOE’s reliance on an undated text exchange as support for its contention that
Respondent triggered the CFDA reporting requirements does not rise to the level of clear and
convincing. The BOE contends that the text exchange proves that Respondent received a
six days late, and knowingly failed to file the required 10-G campaign finance disclosure report, or filed the report
more than eleven days late, then the BOE, functioning as the Supervisory Committee on Campaign Finance
Disclosure, may impose upon the candidate additional civil penalties not to exceed $10,000.00 for each report.
17 La. R.S. 42:1141.5(C). “‘Clear and convincing evidence,’ in general, means that the fact of guilt must be proven to
a greater degree than by ‘a mere preponderance of the evidence’ but less than by ‘beyond a reasonable doubt.’”
Louisiana State Bar Ass’n v. Edwins, 329 So. 2d 437, 442 (La. 1976).
18 La. R.S. 18:1505.1(B).
19 La. R.S. 18:1484.
6

campaign donation in excess of $200. The text exchange indicates that Mr. Thibodeaux and Mr.
Smith spoke before the text exchange, but the BOE did not offer evidence about any conversations
that led to the text exchange. Without context, the text exchange shows only that Mr. Thibodeaux
asked Mr. Smith for specific information and that Mr. Smith regurgitated the information back to
Mr. Thibodeaux. Specifically, Mr. Thibodeaux asked Mr. Smith to “respond to this text that you
no longer have documents relating to the gun and that you estimate the gun you gave to
[Respondent] for the raffle was worth about $300,” and Mr. Smith gave Mr. Thibodeaux what he
asked for, included a “guesstimate” that the firearm had a value of $300 (emphasis added).
The BOE did not offer evidence about the paperwork or documents related to the firearm
that Mr. Smith seems to have had at some point, or why he no longer has them. The BOE did not
offer evidence to show why Mr. Smith is a reliable source for the valuation of a firearm. The BOE
did not offer evidence to show the date of any donation or any other details about a donation. The
BOE did not call Mr. Thibodeaux or Mr. Smith to offer additional information or context at the
hearing. The EAB does not find the text exchange to be credible evidence that Respondent
received a contribution in excess of $200.
The BOE’s reliance on the phone call as support for its contention that Respondent
triggered the CFDA reporting requirements likewise does not rise to the level of clear and
convincing. Critically, the phone call does not specify a single date of a purchase or donation.
Further, the statement in the phone call that the blemished parts are only available “from time to
time” opens the possibility that the parts may have been purchased, and the rifle may have been
made, during a period that did not coincide with Respondent’s 2022 candidacy for Chief of Police,
Town of Pearl River, or that any values assigned to the parts, or to the rifle, may not have been
accurate during any period relevant to Respondent’s 2022 candidacy for Chief of Police, Town of
7

Pearl River. The EAB does not find the phone call to be credible evidence that Respondent
received a contribution in excess of $200 during the relevant time period.
Finally, the BOE did not identify the aggregating period for Respondent’s 2022 candidacy
for Chief of Police, Town of Pearl River. Because the BOE’s SDT limited the period for which it
requested documents from January 1, 2022, through January 31, 2023, the EAB accepts that the
aggregating period began no earlier than January 1, 2022, and ended no later than January 31,
2023. The BOE failed to present any evidence to show when any campaign donation was made.
Therefore, the BOE failed to present any evidence that Respondent received a contribution, of any
amount, during the aggregating period in connection with his 2022 candidacy for Police Chief,
Town of Pearl River.
The evidence does not support a finding that Respondent received a campaign contribution
in excess of $200 in the aggregate during the aggregating period in connection with his 2022
candidacy for Chief of Police, Town of Pearl River. The BOE failed to present credible evidence
to show that Respondent received a contribution in excess of $200, and it failed to present any
evidence of a date that he received any donation. Therefore, the BOE failed to prove by clear and
convincing evidence that Respondent was required to and knowingly failed to file a 10-P and a 10-
G campaign finance disclosure report in connection with his 2022 candidacy for Chief of Police,
Town of Pearl River.
Because the BOE failed to prove that Respondent was required to file 10-P and 10-G
campaign finance disclosure reports, it is not authorized to impose against Respondent any
additional civil penalty under the authority of La. R.S. 18:1505.4(A)(4)(a) and (b).
8

ORDER
IT IS ORDERED that the Louisiana Board of Ethics, in its capacity as the Supervisory
Committee on Campaign Finance Disclosure, failed to prove by clear and convincing evidence
that Kevin E. Casmere was required to file a 10-P or a 10-G campaign finance disclosure report in
connection with his 2022 candidacy for Chief of Police, Town of Pearl River.
IT IS FURTHER ORDERED that the Louisiana Board of Ethics, in its capacity as the
Supervisory Committee on Campaign Finance Disclosure, is not authorized to impose an
additional civil penalty against Kevin E. Casmere for failing to file a 10-P campaign finance
disclosure report.
IT IS FURTHER ORDERED that the Louisiana Board of Ethics, in its capacity as the
Supervisory Committee on Campaign Finance Disclosure, is not authorized to impose an
additional civil penalty against Kevin E. Casmere for failing to file a 10-G campaign finance
disclosure report.

text:

DIVISION OF ADMINISTRATIVE LAW

DECISION AND ORDER
The Louisiana Board of Ethics (BOE), in its capacity as the Supervisory Committee on
Campaign Finance Disclosure, requested an adjudicatory hearing to have the Ethics Adjudicatory
Board (EAB) determine whether Keitron Gagnon knowingly failed to file his 10-P and 30-P
campaign finance disclosure reports by the sixth day after they were due, and his 10-G campaign
finance disclosure report by the eleventh day after it was due, in connection with his 2023
candidacy for the office of Governor, State of Louisiana. The BOE proved by clear and convincing
evidence that Keitron Gagnon knowingly failed to file the reports as alleged. The BOE is
authorized to impose an additional civil penalty not to exceed $10,000 against Keitron Gagnon for
each report pursuant to Louisiana Revised Statutes (La. R.S.) 18:1505.4(A)(4)(a) and (b).
APPEARANCES
An adjudicatory hearing was conducted March 21, 2025, in Baton Rouge, Louisiana,
before Panel A of the EAB.1 Charles Reeves appeared as counsel on behalf of the BOE. Although
duly noticed, Keitron Gagnon (Respondent) did not appear for the hearing.2
1 Panel A of the EAB consists of administrative law judges Cazeline G. Hebert (presiding), Michele L. Staggs, and
Stephanie E. Robin.
2 On December 6, 2024, a Notice of Hearing was mailed by the Administrative Hearings Clerk for the Division of
Administrative Law to Respondent at 837 Melody Drive, Metairie, Louisiana, 70002. This is the same address the
BOE mailed Respondent the charges contained in its Request for Hearing, its Late Fee Assessment Orders, and its
discovery, includingRequests for Admissions, all by certified mail, returned receipt requested, and the BOE received
the certified mail receipts;see BOE Exhibits 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, and 14. This is the same address Respondent listed as
his mailing address on hisNotice of Candidacy (Qualifying Form);see BOE Exhibit 2. Respondent was provided an
additional 15 minutes past the scheduled hearing start time but failed to appear.

JURISDICTIONAL AUTHORITY
The EAB is a legislatively created board, as contemplated by Article X, Section 21, of the
Louisiana Constitution. The EAB has original jurisdiction under La. R.S. 42:1141.5 to determine
whether violations of the Code of Governmental Ethics, La. R.S. 42:1101 et seq., have occurred
and to conduct hearings under La. R.S. 18:1505.4 for specific violations of the Campaign Finance
Disclosure Act (CFDA), La. R.S. 18:1481et seq.
This adjudication is conducted in accordance with the CFDA, the Code of Governmental
Ethics, the Administrative Procedure Act, La. R.S. 49:950 et seq., and the enabling legislation for
the Division of Administrative Law, La. R.S. 49:991 et seq.
STATEMENT OF THE CASE
The BOE, in its capacity as the Supervisory Committee on Campaign Finance Disclosure,
alleged that Respondent failed to file three campaign finance disclosure reports by their deadlines
in connection with his 2023 candidacy for the office of Governor, State of Louisiana.
The BOE requested that the EAB conduct an adjudicatory hearing to determine whether
Respondent knowingly failed to file his 10-P and 30-P campaign finance disclosure reports by the
sixth day after they were due, and his 10-G campaign finance disclosure report by the eleventh day
after it was due, which could subject Respondent to an additional civil penalty not to exceed
$10,000 for each report, pursuant to La. R.S. 18:1505.4(A)(4)(a) and (b).
At the hearing, the BOE offered its exhibits, numbered BOE Exhibits 1 through 13, which
were admitted into evidence.
Counsel presented the case on behalf of the BOE and requested an opportunity to
supplement the record with BOE Exhibit 14, which is the Certified Mail Return Receipt indicating
delivery of the BOE’sRequest for Hearingand discovery mailed to Respondent on July 25, 2024,
2

and delivered on August 1, 2024. The record was held open until March 24, 2025, at 4:30 p.m. to
allow the BOE an opportunity to supplement the hearing record with its additional exhibit.
On March 21, 2025, after the in-person hearing, the BOE submitted a copy of the Certified
Mail Return Receipt showing delivery on August 1, 2024, of the BOE’s Request for Hearingand
discovery mailed to Respondent on July 25, 2024, marked as BOE Exhibit 14, which was admitted
into evidence. The record closed on March 24, 2025.
The matter was taken under advisement for a determination of whether Respondent failed
to file the 10-P, 30-P, and 10-G campaign finance disclosure reports in violation of La. R.S.
18:1495.4(B)(3), La. R.S. 1495.4(B)(4), and La. R.S. 1495.4(B)(5) and would therefore be subject
to additional civil penalties pursuant to La. R.S. 18:1505.4(A)(4)(a) and (b) for each late report.
FINDINGS OF FACT
Respondent qualified to be a candidate for the office of Governor, State of Louisiana, in a
primary election scheduled for October 14, 2023.3 Respondent acknowledged that he was subject
to the provisions of the CFDA when he signed the qualifying form.4 The office of Governor, State
of Louisiana, is a “major” level public office.5 A primary election was held on October 14, 2023.6
Respondent was defeated in the primary election.7 A general election was held November 18,
2023.8 Respondent did not participate in the general election held on November 18, 2023.
On December 7, 2023, the BOE issued two Late Fee Assessment Orders to Respondent
because he had not yet filed his 10-P or his 30-P campaign finance disclosure reports.9 On March
6, 2024, the BOE issued aLate Fee Assessment Order to Respondent because he had not yet filed
3 BOE Exhibit 2.

his 10-G campaign finance disclosure report.10 In the letters accompanying the Late Fee
Assessment Orders, Respondent was notified that he was required to file his 10-P, 30-P, and 10-G
reports and that he could be subject to an additional penalty of $10,000 for each report he failed to
file.11
As of March 7, 2025, Respondent has not filed his 10-P, 30-P, or 10-G campaign finance
disclosure reports12 and, as of March 21, 2025, he has not filed responses to the BOE’s Requests
for Admissions.13
CONCLUSIONS OF LAW
The BOE proved by clear and convincing evidence that Respondent knowingly failed to
file his 10-P and 30-P campaign finance disclosure reports by the sixth day after they were due,
and his 10-G campaign finance disclosure report by the eleventh day after it was due. The BOE
is authorized to impose upon Respondent an additional civil penalty not to exceed $10,000 for
each report, as allowed by La. R.S. 18:1505.4(A)(4)(a) and (b).14
In hearings under the CFDA brought before the EAB, the BOE must prove by clear and
convincing evidence that the candidate knowingly failed to timely file a required campaign finance
disclosure report.15 Failure to timely submit the requisite reports constitutes a violation of the
CFDA.16

or 10-G campaign finance disclosure reports.

EAB determines that a candidate knowingly failed to file the required 10-P and 30-P reports, or filed the 10-P and 30-
P reports more than six days late, and knowingly failed to file the required 10-G campaign finance disclosure report,
or filed the report more than eleven days late, then the BOE, functioning as the Supervisory Committee on Campaign
Finance Disclosure, may impose upon the candidate additional civil penalties not to exceed $10,000.00 for each report.
15 La. R.S. 42:1141.5(C). “‘Clear and convincing evidence’, in general, means that the fact of guilt must be proven to
a greater degree than by ‘a mere preponderance of the evidence’ but less than by ‘beyond a reasonable doubt.’”
Louisiana State Bar Ass’n v. Edwins, 329 So. 2d 437, 442 (La. 1976).
16 La. R.S. 18:1505.1(B).

The office of Governor, State of Louisiana, is a “major” level public office.17 Every
candidate for a “major” level public office (or their campaign treasurer) is required to file certain
campaign finance disclosure reports by the statutory deadlines.18
As a candidate for Governor, State of Louisiana, a “major” level public office, Respondent
was required to file a 30-P report by September 14, 2023, which was the 30th day prior to the
primary election on October 14, 2023.19 Respondent was also required to file a 10-P report by
October 4, 2023, which was the 10th day prior to the primary election on October 14, 2023.20
Lastly, Respondent was required to file a final 10-G report by November 8, 2023, which was the
10th day prior to the general election on November 18, 2023.21 As of March 7, 2025, Respondent
has not filed the 30-P, 10-P, or 10-G campaign finance disclosure reports.
In connection with his 2023 candidacy for the office of Governor, State of Louisiana,
Respondent knew he was obligated to meet the CFDA filing requirements by the statutory
deadlines and that additional civil penalties, not to exceed $10,000 per report, could be imposed if
he did not file the 30-P, 10-P, or 10-G campaign finance disclosure reports. The BOE proved by
clear and convincing evidence that Respondent knowingly failed to file the 30-P, 10-P, and 10-G
campaign finance disclosure reports by the statutory deadlines.
Additionally, Respondent’s failure to file the 30-P, 10-P, and 10-G campaign finance
disclosure reports within three days after the final date for filing creates a rebuttable presumption
of intent to not file the reports.22 No evidence was offered to rebut this statutory presumption.
If, after conducting an adjudicatory hearing, the EAB determines that Respondent

knowingly failed to file the requisite campaign finance disclosure reports by the sixth and the
eleventh day after the reports were due, respectively, then the BOE may impose an additional civil
penalty, not to exceed $10,000, against Respondent for each report that he failed to timely file.23
The BOE proved by clear and convincing evidence that Respondent, a candidate for a
“major” level office, knowingly violated the CFDA by failing to file his 30-P, 10-P, and 10-G
campaign finance disclosure reports by the statutory deadlines and by the sixth day and eleventh
day after the reports were due, respectively.
In connection with his 2023 candidacy for the office of Governor, State of Louisiana, the
BOE, in its capacity as the Supervisory Committee for Campaign Finance Disclosure, is authorized
to impose against Respondent an additional civil penalty under authority of La. R.S.
18:1505.4(A)(4)(a) and (b), not to exceed $10,000 for each report.
ORDER
IT IS ORDERED that the Louisiana Board of Ethics, in its capacity as the Supervisory
Committee on Campaign Finance Disclosure, is authorized to impose an additional civil penalty
not to exceed $10,000 against Keitron Gagnon, in connection with his 2023 candidacy for the
office of Governor, State of Louisiana, for failing to file his 30-P campaign finance disclosure
report by the sixth day after it was due.
IT IS FURTHER ORDERED that the Louisiana Board of Ethics, in its capacity as the
Supervisory Committee on Campaign Finance Disclosure, is authorized to impose an additional
civil penalty not to exceed $10,000 against Keitron Gagnon, in connection with his 2023 candidacy
for the office of Governor, State of Louisiana, for failing to file his 10-P campaign finance
disclosure report by the sixth day after it was due.
